title: A new high-resolution daily mean South China Sea Ocean Reanalysis dataset: SCSORA
abstract: This research presents a high-resolution ocean reanalysis dataset for the South China Sea covering 2001 to 2024. The dataset assimilates satellite remote sensing data and in-situ observations. It provides daily mean three-dimensional fields of temperature, salinity, currents, and sea surface height. Validation results show good agreement with observations. The dataset has been used to support studies of marine heatwaves, mesoscale eddies, and related processes in this important region.

title: Comparing Data-Driven and Numerical Weather Prediction Forecasts of Extreme Weather: A Review
abstract: arXiv:2611.23863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data-driven weather forecasting models, chiefly trained on reanalysis data, now match or beat physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) models on most headline scores, but whether this advantage extends to extreme weather is contested. We review peer-reviewed studies that directly compare data-driven forecasts with NWP for extremes, from nowcasting to subseasonal lead times. We discuss grey literature in the outlook but do not include it in the formal review. There is good agreement on the fact that data-driven models mostly outperform NWP on temperature extremes, tropical cyclone tracks and the location of synoptic features across time scales. The evidence is mixed for extreme precipitation and feature-based extreme event detection such as extremes related to atmospheric rivers, while it leans toward better NWP performance for estimating event intensity. For record-breaking events that lie outside the training distribution, the evidence is narrower. Nonetheless, both a systematic global evaluation and several case studies find that physics-based models retain the advantage, with data-driven models underestimating both the frequency and the magnitude of records. Hybrid systems that post-process NWP with machine-learning (ML), or couple data-driven forecasts with physics-based models, deliver some of the largest and most consistent gains. We argue that headline scores, verification choices and case selection explain much of the apparent disagreement in the literature, and provide recommendations for a more trustworthy and interpretable evaluation of data-driven models for extreme and record-breaking weather.

title: How abruptly did the Holocene Green Sahara end?
abstract: To move the long-standing debate of whether the vegetation changes in the Sahara during the last 8000 years occurred abruptly or gradually we propose a new quantitative metric. Our analysis of model and proxy data suggests the vegetation composition in the Holocene Sahara can undergo substantially more abrupt transitions than total vegetation cover, and a gradual expansion of the Sahara can be accompanied by abrupt, step-like transitions within local ecosystems.

title: Run it Back: Autoregression vs. Video Diffusion for Final-Conditioned Weather Trajectories
abstract: arXiv:2611.21521v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Low-likelihood, high-impact extremes are projected to increase in severity and frequency in a warming climate. Sampling the precursors that lead to these events traditionally requires massive ensembles that scale poorly with lead time and rarity, and typical rare-event sampling and ensemble-boosting methods do not show how a single extreme might arise from diverse synoptic precursors. Recently, Lin et al.\ (2026) showed this is possible with final-conditioned 66-hour trajectories (trajectories constrained to end at an observed state) from cBottle-video, a pre-trained, off-the-shelf video diffusion climate emulator not explicitly fine-tuned for this task (Brenowitz et al., 2025). However, its ensembles were underdispersed and geostrophically inconsistent, and it reproduces conditioned frames only approximately, hindering autoregressive rollout. Here, we train Rewind-AR, a backward-in-time probabilistic autoregressive model with a FourCastNet~3 backbone (Bonev et al., 2025), and generate final-conditioned ensembles for the same three cases: the 2021 Pacific Northwest heatwave, Hurricane Ian, and Superstorm Sandy (in the Supplementary Information). The leading modes of Rewind-AR's antecedent 500 hPa geopotential height explain far more of the across-member variance than cBottle-video's for both hurricane position and heatwave surface temperature, and Rewind-AR better reproduces the day-over-day heatwave intensification observed in ERA5. Finally, geostrophic inconsistencies close to the conditioning frame seen in cBottle-video are not reproduced by Rewind-AR. Nevertheless, up to 22\% of Rewind-AR members become numerically unstable within 66 hours, so improving rollout physical consistency and stability over long lead times is a natural next step.

title: Quantifying the role of temporal-scale-dependent precipitation change in mass balance in the Dongkemadi Glacier, Tibetan Plateau
abstract: Understanding how precipitation changes affect glaciers is critical for predicting their future responses as well as for forecasting water supplies and potential impacts on downstream lowland regions. This study evaluated the effects of precipitation changes at annual, seasonal, and monthly scales on the mass balance of the Dongkemadi (DKMD) Glacier (central Tibetan Plateau) during 1960–2009. Results showed increasing trends in precipitation at the annual, seasonal, and monthly scales, except in July (decreasing trend). Warm season (i.e., the glacier’s melt season) precipitation constituted 91.4% of annual precipitation, and accounted for 80.3% of the annual precipitation increase. A comparison of precipitation changes effects across the three scales revealed: i) All three precipitation trends increased annual, warm season and monthly glacier mass balance, except in July; ii) Using monthly precipitation trends captured the monthly variability of precipitation-induced mass balance changes (range: 50 mm w.e.); iii) Annual or seasonal precipitation trends underestimated mass balance changes by approximately 22%; iv) The direct driver of mass balance increase was enhanced mass inputs (i.e., snowfall) from increased precipitation, which accounted for over half of the total increase in mass balance; and v) The indirect driver was reduced melt energy, primarily attributed to decreased net shortwave radiation caused by higher surface albedo. This study confirms the effectiveness of using monthly precipitation trends to investigate how precipitation changes impacted on the DKMD Glacier and its meltwater runoff. Furthermore, it provides valuable insights for accurately assessing precipitation changes effects on the energy and mass balance of glaciers globally.

title: WeatherDreamer: Learning a World Model from Multimodal Earth Observations
abstract: arXiv:2611.18393v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine learning weather models now rival operational global forecasts but still start from analyses produced by separate, expensive data assimilation (DA) systems, which for global models are typically updated every six hours. Observation-to-observation models avoid this dependence, but most omit the recursive filtering cycle that lets DA systems carry a background state through sparse, irregular observations. We introduce WeatherDreamer, a world model that learns this cycle end-to-end from 18 global observing systems, without reanalysis. It infers a latent state from observations, carries it forward hour by hour with learned dynamics, corrects it each hour with new observations, and can predict what any of its observing systems would measure at any location. At held-out stations, its ensembles beat NOAA's Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) for temperature, dew point and wind out to 12 h and are better calibrated than GEFS and the ECMWF ensemble. Precipitation, cloud-top height and solar irradiance, never inputs at inference, are inferred with skill matching or exceeding operational products at short leads. Against the first guess of NOAA's Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) DA system, WeatherDreamer's short-range departures are within 10% of GSI's at surface stations and within 25% for moisture-sensitive microwave channels, but up to five times larger for temperature-sounding channels. Never given observation errors, its learned update assumes errors close to known instrument and retrieval errors of microwave sounders and scatterometer winds. WeatherDreamer also separates viewing geometry from atmospheric state, recovering 83-96% of observed limb darkening and producing seamless nadir-view imagery. Producing an hourly global analysis in about 1.5 minutes on one GPU, WeatherDreamer shows that assimilation and forecasting can be learned together directly from observations.

Review Article: A Systematic Review of Acquisition and Processing Approaches for Earth Observations of Arctic Sea Ice Melt Ponds
abstract: This review article explains how scientists monitor Arctic melt ponds, which are pools of water that form on sea ice in late spring and early summer. These ponds absorb more sunlight than ice, speeding up melting and reinforcing warming. We examine satellite and field measurements, compare the strengths and limits of different tools, and review available datasets. The study highlights current knowledge gaps and identifies priorities to improve future observations and climate predictions.

title: Improved CMIP6 projections of Hudson Bay region navigability using bias correction and route continuity
abstract: Hudson Bay’s seasonal sea ice limits maritime access to the Port of Churchill, and although we know future warming will lengthen the navigable period, how quickly it will lengthen is unclear. Based on several methods for making future projections, the navigable period for the route from Churchill to the Labrador Sea has lengthened by about 4 weeks since the 1980s. In the future, it is projected to lengthen by about 2 weeks for each additional 0.5 °C of global warming.

title: Climate suitability of East Asian mangroves for nature-based solutions is limited by climate extremes
abstract: Mangroves store carbon and protect coasts. We used satellite images and climate models to assess how changing conditions affect mangroves in East Asia. Sunlight and winter temperatures were linked to leaf greenness, sometimes months later. Warming may make northern areas more suitable, but more frequent periods of low sunlight under high emissions could limit these benefits. Conservation and restoration planning should consider both temperature and sunlight, as well as local habitat conditions.

title: Uncertainty Estimate for Extended Reconstructed Sea Surface Temperature Version 6 (ERSSTv6)
abstract: Abstract The NOAA Extended Reconstructed Sea Surface Temperature version 6 (ERSSTv6) provides a globally complete monthly SST dataset from 1850 to present, reconstructed from ship, buoy, and near-surface Argo observations using an artificial neural network (ANN) approach. ERSSTv6 incorporates enhanced quality control, large-scale spatial filtering, and an updated ice–SST proxy and includes an operationally feasible and physically consistent uncertainty framework that supports robust assessments of SST variability, trends, and ocean-related applications. We quantify total SST uncertainty as the combination of parametric and reconstruction uncertainties. Parametric uncertainty is estimated from a 1000-member ensemble generated by perturbing 30 internal parameters, including ANN coefficients, quality control, bias adjustments, and ice-SST proxy. ANN-related uncertainty is approximated using a random perturbation (RP) to ANN coefficients, whose magnitude is calibrated by validation errors. Reconstruction uncertainty is assessed with a 500-member ensemble applied to a space-time-complete reference dataset, representing algorithmic error under ideal observations. Results show that grid-scale uncertainty is largest in regions with strong SST variability and sparse data, including western boundary currents, the eastern equatorial Pacific, and ice-covered areas, with global mean uncertainty decreasing from 0.4°–0.5°C in the 1850s to ∼0.3°C after 1950. Uncertainty in global mean SST is smaller, ranging from 0.06°–0.08°C in the 1850s to ∼0.02°C in recent decades. Factor analysis indicates that ANN RP dominates the grid-scale uncertainty, while ship bias correction and ice–SST proxy dominate the uncertainty of global-mean SST. Comparisons show that both SST and its uncertainty in ERSSTv6 are broadly consistent with those other SST products.

title: Climate and glacier geometry dominate global glacier–lake interactions
abstract: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02808-5 The contribution of glacial lakes to glacier mass loss is unclear. This work maps global glacial lakes in 2000 and 2020 to quantify changes in number, volume and area, showing that they explain 11 ± 7% of lake-terminating glacier loss, with climate forcing and glacier geometry the dominant factors.

title: Seasonal biases induced by illumination changes and shadow casting in remote sensing derived glacier flow velocities
abstract: Sub-annual glacier surface velocity derived from remote sensing images are receiving increasing attention. In the meantime, systematic seasonal errors (i.e. biases) have been reported in time series derived from optical images on various landforms, such as landslides or dunes. The extent to which such biases affect glacier velocity maps remains poorly investigated. Here, we propose characterizing the amplitude and spatial distribution of these seasonal biases.

title: Retreating glaciers and snow cover are amplifying summer droughts in the upper Adige River Basin (Italy)
journal: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
abstract: Snow and glacier meltwater play a critical role in sustaining summer streamflow in mountains and downstream regions. Yet, understanding glaciers' contributions to buffer river streamflow during droughts remains limited and poses major barriers to improve present and future water management within the context of climate change. This study evaluates the contribution of glacier melt to summer flows and its role in mitigating hydrological droughts in the upper Adige River basin (Italy). We developed and implemented a new dynamic glacier module into the ICHYMOD-TOPMELT hydrological model, annually updating glacier area and improving the quantification of meltwater contributions under progressive glacier retreat (from 111 km 2 in 1997 to 79 km 2 in 2017). The hydrological model exhibited robust performance (KGE = 0.89 for 1997–2022 for the whole upper Adige River basin at the Bronzolo closing station; 0.88 in summers) capturing observed glacier area, mass balance, and seasonal melt trends. Results show that glacier melt in the upper Adige River basin contributed an average of 4.5 % to total summer streamflow during 1997–2022, with significant spatial variability, reaching 30 % in glacierized subbasins. During the severe droughts of 2003, 2005 and 2022, glacier melt contributions ranged between 4 % and 12 % at the upper Adige closing section. In 2003, high temperature and limited Snow Water Equivalent (SWE) led to glacier melt accounting for 11.67 % of summer flows. By contrast, the significant runoff deficit in 2005 was driven by colder temperatures, which reduced glacier melt contributions to 4.85 %, combined with low SWE conditions. In 2022, the combination of low precipitation, low snow cover and high temperature drove glacier melt. In contrast to the 2003 drought, reduced glacier areas led to lower absolute contributions (8.17 %). Our findings reveal that despite the increased melt rates in recent warm years, retreating glacier areas have reduced their absolute buffering effect. Glacier retreat is weakening the contribution of glaciers to summer flows, increasing the upper Adige River basin's dependence on precipitation and snowmelt, the latter of which is also showing a decreasing trend. For these reasons, accounting for dynamic glacier and snow changes is essential to improve future drought projections and inform adaptive water management in glacier-fed basins within the context of climate and anthropogenic changes.

North Atlantic Modulation of the 1931 Extreme East Asian Summer Flood Revealed by Large-Ensemble Seasonal Forecasts
abstract: Extreme precipitation during May-July 1931 caused severe flooding over East Asia, with devastating societal impacts. The mechanisms and predictability of this event remain uncertain because sparse early-twentieth-century observations limit robust attribution based on a single reanalysis realization. Here, we use a century-long 51-member CSF-20C seasonal hindcast to examine the predictability and dynamical drivers of the 1931 flood from an ensemble perspective. In this framework, the ensemble mean represents the predictable signal, whereas the inter-member spread represents the unpredictable component that is not constrained by the common initial conditions. The ensemble mean reproduces the tropical Indo-Pacific SST anomalies and the western North Pacific anomalous anticyclone, but the predicted rainband is displaced southward relative to observations, indicating that the predictable signal alone is insufficient to determine the observed rainband location. Individual members that better reproduce the observed rainfall pattern reveal a key role for extratropical modulation. The leading inter-member EOF mode explains 50.06% of the precipitation spread over eastern China and is associated with a Eurasian mid- to high-latitude wave train linked to a North Atlantic tripole-like SST pattern. This wave train modulates the East Asian upper-level jet, enhances ascent over eastern China, and shifts the rainband northward toward its observed location. Surface turbulent heat-flux anomalies and idealized linear baroclinic model experiments further support the physical plausibility of a North Atlantic influence. These results indicate that the 1931 flood arose from a predictable signal whose regional expression was modulated by North Atlantic-related extratropical circulation variability. Our study based on large-sample seasonal hindcasts offers a transferable framework for attributing extreme climate events.

title: Discrepancies and Consistencies in Multi-Source Estimates of Eurasian Spring Snowmelt During 1982–2014
abstract: Snow alters land–atmosphere energy and moisture exchanges via albedo and hydrological effects, markedly impacting subseasonal-to-seasonal climate variability. While Earth observations and model-based products form the foundation for investigating snow–climate interactions, comprehensive assessments of snowmelt, which directly reflects snow-induced hydrological and thermal anomalies, remain scarce compared to those of conventional snow mass variables. Benchmarked against the satellite–in situ blended GlobSnow data, this study comprehensively evaluates the discrepancies and consistencies of Eurasian spring snowmelt (spring snow water equivalent difference, SSD) across six multi-source datasets (SnowCCI, JRA-3Q, ERA5-Land, MERRA-2, GLDAS-NOAH, and FLDAS) during 1982–2014. The results reveal that satellite-based SnowCCI and JRA-3Q exhibit the highest consistency with GlobSnow in reproducing the spatial distribution, temporal variability, and dominant east–west dipole mode of Eurasian SSD. Specifically, they accurately capture its clear latitudinal zonation and a distinct dipole-like trend, characterized by decreasing SSD over western Eurasia and increasing SSD over eastern Eurasia. Conversely, ERA5-Land and MERRA-2 reasonably capture the temporal evolution of SSD but tend to overestimate variability amplitudes. GLDAS-NOAH exhibits relatively weak regional heterogeneity and underestimates SSD variability, whereas FLDAS tends to overestimate variability amplitudes and shows pronounced regional dependence. Further analysis suggests that uncertainties in snowfall simulations may be a major source of discrepancies in SSD estimation, although their relative contribution remains uncertain. These findings provide crucial insights for selecting appropriate datasets in snow–climate research and underscore the importance of dataset uncertainty quantification in subseasonal-to-seasonal climate prediction.

title: A global 0.05° dataset of daily latent heat flux and resistances (2001–2020) derived via the Energy-Resistance-Coupling framework
abstract: Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) We developed a daily global dataset describing latent heat flux and the resistances that regulate land–atmosphere water and energy exchange from 2001 to 2020 at 0.05° resolution. The product was evaluated against 244 flux-tower sites and performs robustly across climates and ecosystems. It provides new information for studying drought, ecosystem water stress, land–atmosphere coupling, and Earth system models.

title: Tracing Uncertainties of Extreme El Ni\~{n}o Prediction to Mesoscale Ocean Currents
abstract: arXiv:2611.17854v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The predictability of the El Ni\~{n}o-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) has historically been linked to large-scale errors in models' initial conditions such as heat content and surface wind stress. Here we demonstrate that these slowly evolving errors may ultimately originate from mesoscale errors in initial oceanic states that are common in current models and ocean observation systems. This hidden source of ENSO forecast uncertainty, in terms of mesoscale ocean-current errors, is convincingly exposed by the conditional nonlinear optimal perturbation (CNOP) method applied to a differentiable ocean AI model. The CNOP-identified most influential current errors are strongly event-dependent. For the 1997/98 El Ni\~{n}o, the initial current errors in the eastern Pacific results in the largest forecast error through locally suppressing original subsurface warming. For the 2015/16 event, the dominate error originates from the western Pacific, which reorganizes upper ocean temperature structure and affects the eastern Pacific through the equatorial waveguide. Further analysis reveals that these current errors perturb mesoscale eddy count and eddy kinetic energy triggering large-scale temperature errors that hinder El Ni\~{n}o development. The timing of the maximum growth rate of the obtained CNOP error is well aligned with the spring predictability barrier of ENSO, and the error structures are reflected in simulated analysis errors caused by unresolved mesoscale currents. These findings extend the potential source of ENSO predictability beyond large-scale thermal signals, reveal for the first time an uncharted route of ENSO forecast failure, and provide an important physical basis for targeted ocean observations and data assimilation in the future.

title: GPU-accelerated atmospheric chemical kinetics using single precision in the ECHAM/MESSy (EMAC) model v2.55 with MEDINA v2.0
abstract: We address a major bottleneck in Earth system models, the high computational cost of simulating atmospheric chemical reactions, using graphics processing units. The MEDINA code-to-code compiler supports switching from double-precision to single-precision arithmetic on the accelerator, reducing average processing times by 30 %. Tests showed that this more efficient approach maintains high accuracy, with results matching traditional methods within 0.004 %.

title: The ocean–atmosphere turbulent flux algorithm in E3SMv2 does not always converge to unique and physical solutions:  analysis and potential remedy
abstract: Accurately computing ocean–atmosphere turbulent fluxes, which measure the transfer of momentum, heat, and water between the Earth and its oceans, in Earth system models is important for overall model accuracy. Under certain meteorological conditions, the set of equations utilized in many Earth system models to parameterize these fluxes can have no solution or more than one solution. Modifying the equations to address these issues leads to substantial changes to the simulated turbulent fluxes.

title: Learning Calibrated and Samplable Predictive Distributions of Surface-Ocean $\Delta p$CO$_2$ Using Tabular Diffusion Models
abstract: arXiv:2611.21769v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The ocean absorbs almost 30% of anthropogenic CO$_2$ emissions, but quantifying this sink requires estimating surface-ocean CO$_2$ from observations that are sparse in space and time. Most existing machine-learning estimates of this field are deterministic, giving a single value per grid point, with uncertainty approximated post hoc via residuals, ensembles, or prescribed distributions. We instead learn a conditional predictive distribution for each observation: using Treeffuser, a conditional diffusion model with gradient-boosted-tree score functions, we estimate the full predictive distribution of $\Delta p$CO$_2$ (the sea-air $p$CO$_2$ difference) from 13 environmental, spatial, and temporal predictors. On a held-out SOCAT test set, Treeffuser attains the lowest continuous ranked probability score among the uncertainty-quantification methods evaluated (8.229 $\mu$atm) and the coverage closest to the nominal 68% / 95% levels (0.686 / 0.930), while retaining point-prediction skill comparable to a deterministic XGBoost baseline (RMSE 18.4 vs. 17.7 $\mu$atm; $R^2$ 0.77 vs. 0.79). These results show that conditional diffusion can provide well-calibrated, observation-level uncertainties while largely preserving point-prediction skill. Because Treeffuser is generative, its samples can support probabilistic analyses of $\Delta p$CO$_2$; extending this to spatially coherent field reconstruction will require modeling dependence across grid cells and evaluation on spatially held-out data.

title: Daily melt pond and net ice surface fractions in the Arctic Ocean from MODIS visible imagery: 2000–2024
abstract: Melt ponds form during summer on Arctic sea ice. They impact the amount of solar energy entering the sea ice-ocean system. We describe the retrieval method of a new data set of the daily melt-pond coverage on Arctic sea ice north of 60 degrees latitude North for June to August of years 2000 to 2024 based on satellite remote sensing. The results of the quality assessment against independent observations demonstrate the data set’s credibility and usefulness for Arctic climate system studies.

title: The 4-mode Modal Aerosol Module in C+ +  (MAM4xx) v1.0: representing prognostic aerosols in a global cloud-system resolving atmosphere model for GPU exascale computing
abstract: We ported a prognostic representation of aerosols to C++ and integrated it into an Earth system model that runs on powerful GPU supercomputers. The code conversion approach keeps the same detailed physics as the Fortran version, was carefully tested, and results show that new code produces aerosol simulations consistent with real‑world data over the central U.S. in spring 2016. Future work will optimize the code for GPUs so to reduce the overall computational time.

title: Urban climate dynamics in informal settlements: Spatiotemporal rainfall and temperature variability in Thembelihle, Johannesburg
abstract: by Sailas Hussein Matamanda, Walter Musakwa, Armstrong Dzomba Climate change has emerged as a critical contemporary concern, marked by greater variability and severity in weather systems, from extreme heat to drought and intense precipitation. Africa is particularly vulnerable, with urban settlements facing disproportionate risks. This study investigates long-term temperature and rainfall dynamics in Thembelihle, an informal settlement in Johannesburg, alongside broader metropolitan trends, using robust statistical and geospatial methods. Temperature and rainfall data spanning five decades (1974–2024 for Thembelihle; 1981–2024 for Johannesburg) were examined using the non-parametric Mann-Kendall (MK) Test and Sen’s Slope estimation to detect monotonic trends. Rainfall indices included the number of wet days (NWDT), the highest number of consecutive wet days (HNCWD), the highest number of consecutive dry days (HNCDD), and the maximum daily rainfall (HRPD). Extreme temperature events in Thembelihle were examined using a Peak Over Threshold (POT) approach. Spatial interpolation of CHIRPS rainfall and ERA5 temperature anomalies was conducted in QGIS to visualize spatiotemporal variability across Johannesburg. Results reveal statistically significant warming in Thembelihle, with minimum temperatures increasing at 0.0505 °C/year and maximum temperatures at 0.0391 °C/year, remaining higher than Johannesburg’s anomaly trend, although the magnitude of this difference is reduced when trends are compared over a harmonised temporal baseline (1981–2024). Extreme heat events, though historically rare, have clustered in recent years, signalling emerging instability. Rainfall patterns in Thembelihle show high interannual variability with no significant long-term decline, though spring rainfall exhibits a borderline decreasing trend. Johannesburg’s rainfall metrics highlight intensifying extremes: longer dry spells (+1 day/year) and higher maximum daily rainfall (+0.30 mm/year). Drought analysis identifies overlapping severe years (1984, 1999, 2003), underscoring regional susceptibility, while Thembelihle’s higher variability points to localized vulnerability. Spatial analysis confirms rainfall gradients, with wetter conditions in the northeast and drier conditions in the south, alongside localized temperature hotspots. These findings demonstrate a dual climate challenge: accelerating heat stress and increasingly variable rainfall. Informal settlements such as Thembelihle are disproportionately exposed, requiring both water resource coordination and localized adaptation strategies.

title: Hydroclimatic evolution under changing westerly–monsoon influences in northeastern China since the Late Glacial
abstract: Hydroclimatic variability in the transition zone between the East Asian summer monsoon and mid-latitude westerlies reflects the combined influence of these two circulation systems. Understanding how their relative influences have changed over time is essential for interpreting long-term regional moisture variability. Here, we reconstructed regional hydroclimatic changes since 14.3 ka BP using a continuous lacustrine sequence from Aranji Nur, a closed lake on the southwestern margin of the Hulunbuir Grassland in northeastern China. Sediment grain-size distributions were analyzed and compared with regional paleoclimate and environmental records. Four major hydroclimatic stages were identified: relatively dry conditions during 14.3-9.2 ka BP, increased effective moisture during 9.2-4.8 ka BP, gradually declining moisture during 4.8-1.5 ka BP, and renewed aridification since 1.5 ka BP. Variations in sediment grain size, particularly sand content, were broadly consistent with changes in regional moisture availability and surface stability, reflecting the combined effects of vegetation cover, sediment availability, aeolian transport, and local depositional processes. Comparison with regional records suggests that increased moisture availability during the early to middle Holocene was associated with stronger monsoonal influence and potentially additional moisture supplied by the westerlies. Subsequent drying coincided with weakening monsoonal influence and changes in the position of the westerly jet that may have reduced effective moisture transport to the study region. These findings highlight the importance of both circulation intensity and spatial changes in atmospheric circulation and associated moisture transport pathways in shaping long-term hydroclimatic evolution across the westerly-monsoon transition zone.

title: Extreme-Amplitude MJO Events: Multi-scale Origins and Amplified Role in Compound Extremes
abstract: The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO), the dominant mode of tropical intraseasonal climate variability, significantly influences global weather. It often departs from a regular cycle, exhibiting erratic behavior that occasionally amplifies into exceptionally high-amplitude events, whose characteristics and global impacts remain poorly constrained. Here, we show that boreal winter extreme-amplitude MJO (EA-MJO) events, whose amplitude measured by convection-based MJO indices exceeds the 90th percentile of the historical distribution, arise from enhanced energy transfer to planetary scales, leading to a zonal spatial expansion of MJO. Integrated observational analysis and theoretical modeling reveal that this expansion is facilitated by combined effects of favorable background states and high-frequency transients. Specifically, a concurrent eastward extension of the Indo-Pacific warm pool provides a sustained high-moisture corridor that supports organized convection and promotes MJO intensification by consuming background moisture. Meanwhile, a suppression of westward-propagating high-frequency equatorial Rossby waves from central-to-western Pacific reduces destructive interference, enabling farther eastward MJO propagation and triggering the onset of EA-MJO events. Compared to moderate MJO events, EA-MJOs substantially increase the occurrence of concurrent climate extremes, triggering more frequent compound wet-cold extremes and hot-dry extremes across different regions of China. The revealed multi-scale interaction governing EA-MJO genesis, fueled by low-frequency oceanic states and triggered by high-frequency wave variability, charts a tangible course toward their subseasonal-to-seasonal predictability, with direct implications for early warning of high-impact compound extremes.

title: A regime dependent parameterization of the refractive-index structure parameter $C_n^2$
abstract: arXiv:2611.22641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vertical profiles of the refractive-index (RI) structure parameter, $C_n^2$, are required in atmospheric-optics calculations. The Hufnagel--Valley (HV) model is a useful reference profile and it is widely used however, it is difficult to say that it produces consistent results at the observed altitude, magnitude, and thickness of all turbulent layers and it can diverge from realistic measurements in particular height ranges, sites, and stability regimes. This study develops a regime-dependent RI structure parameter considering meteorological conditions and, more importantly, it provides a structure that can be calibrated against measured $C_n^2$ throughout the surface layer (SL), atmospheric boundary layer (ABL), and free atmosphere. The formulation combines SL including distinct unstable, near-neutral, and stable limits; convective ABL; and free-atmospheric turbulence when kinetic-energy and temperature-variance dissipation rates are available. The $C_n^2$ is formed by weighting the contribution of different layers. We use representative, physically plausible meteorological profiles to examine the model's limiting behavior, transitions between atmospheric regimes, continuity, sensitivity to its parameters, and propagation-related differences from the HV 5/7 model. The intended outcome is a measurement-calibrated model that remains physically interpretable across meteorological regimes.

abstract: arXiv:2611.25075v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bangladesh, home to nearly 178 million people, is highly vulnerable to recurring droughts that threaten food security and rural livelihoods. Machine-learning and deep-learning models are increasingly used to forecast drought indices such as the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI). Most studies report accuracy without a persistence reference, although accumulated indices are strongly autocorrelated, and seldom test drought detection, longer leads or variation between training runs. This study forecast SPEI at 3-, 6- and 12-month timescales one to three months ahead for the eight divisions of Bangladesh, using ERA5 reanalysis checked against 35 Bangladesh Meteorological Department stations. Five models, XGBoost, CNN, Bi-LSTM, CNN-BiLSTM and CEEMDAN-BiLSTM, were trained with five seeds each, scored on accuracy, skill against persistence and drought detection, and interpreted with Shapley values. At a one-month lead, the CNN-BiLSTM and Bi-LSTM beat persistence clearly at SPEI-3 and SPEI-6 (skill 0.408 and 0.350), while at SPEI-12 a Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.872 barely exceeded persistence (0.850). Skill and detection could disagree: at SPEI-3 and a three-month lead, XGBoost had the highest skill (0.439) yet detected none of the 119 drought months. Only at SPEI-6 did the forecasts beat persistence significantly and match its detection at all three leads, with fewer false alarms. At SPEI-12, gains were small or absent and varied between seeds. The forecasts kept 76-80% of their correlation against station-derived SPEI and relied mainly on precipitation and lagged SPEI. Forecasts should therefore be judged on skill against persistence and detection across several seeds, not on accuracy alone. In Bangladesh, SPEI-6 forecasts can support early warning up to three months ahead and SPEI-3 forecasts one month ahead, while SPEI-12 is better suited to monitoring.

title: Bridging the knowledge gaps: A global mapping of capacity building offerings on climate change and health
abstract: by Jaafar Tfayli, Sara Kassab, Zahraa Chamseddine, Shadi Saleh, Nour El Arnaout Climate change is an escalating global health threat with disproportionate effects in climate-vulnerable regions. Building capacity at the intersection of climate and health is essential to equip healthcare systems and professionals to assess risks and sustain resilient services. This study maps online publicly accessible capacity-building offerings on climate change and health, focusing on accessibility and applicability to the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region. A rapid web mapping review identified courses, non-accredited certificates, accredited certificates, and diplomas offered by universities and institutions, excluding master's and PhD programs. Learning outcomes/objectives and metadata (provider type, geography, modality, language, credentialing) were extracted and thematically coded to characterize targeted domains. Twenty-two offerings were identified. Most were courses 82% (n = 18), followed by non-accredited certificates 9% (n = 2), accredited certificates 4.5% (n = 1), and diplomas 4.5% (n = 1). Providers included academic institutions 50% (n = 11), international organizations 27% (n = 6), and e-learning platforms 23% (n = 5). Delivery was predominantly online, 77% (n = 17), with some hybrid, 23% (n = 5) (Fig 2A). Nearly all offerings were in English, 96% (n = 21), with one multilingual; none were in Arabic. Provider geography was largely global (n = 13) or based in the United States (n = 6), with isolated entries from Germany (n = 1), Australia (n = 1), and Kenya (n = 1). No offerings originated from the MENA region. Thematically, programs emphasized climate Change and health policy, governance, leadership, and health impacts, while equity, resilience, competency alignment, applied operations, and stackable credentialing were minimally addressed. Overall, the landscape remains fragmented and rooted in the global north. Key gaps include co-designed, practice-oriented training with climate-vulnerable regions, especially MENA, embedding clear competencies, authentic assessment, and multilingual accessibility.

title: Projection of global daily CO2 emissions in 2026
abstract: arXiv:2611.22406v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Global fossil-fuel combustion and industrial-process CO2 emissions remain close to historical highs, yet the recent slowdown in growth is difficult to assess before conventional inventories become available. We project emissions for 2026 and examine daily departures during major climate and energy disruptions. Carbon Monitor activity-based estimates from 1 January 2019 to 30 September 2026 are combined with Prophet projections for 1 October to 31 December across 47 region-sector series. Global emissions are estimated at 38.1 Gt CO2 in 2026, 36.6 Mt CO2 (+0.10%) above 2025. The reference 68% range for the year-on-year rate is +0.011% to +0.18%. Five September-cutoff hindcasts show lower daily forecast errors for Prophet than for a seasonal-naive benchmark. Regional increases total 0.32 Gt and decreases total 0.29 Gt, so 94.0% of the 0.61 Gt gross movement cancels in the global sum. China contributes the largest reduction (-0.19 Gt), concentrated in industry and ground transport, whereas India contributes the largest increase (+0.19 Gt), led by power and industry. Heat-period power anomalies differ among countries and can be muted by summer averaging, while aviation and shipping show different disruption and recovery profiles. Resolving the near-zero global change reveals where reductions are concentrated and where continued growth offsets them, providing a timely basis for assessing the breadth of mitigation progress.

title: Associations of long-term and short-term summertime temperature with survival among patients with cardiovascular disease: A UK-wide retrospective cohort study
abstract: by Ka Yan Lai, Chris Webster, John Gallacher, Chinmoy Sarkar Evidence examining the long-term and acute effects of summertime temperature on survival among patients with cardiovascular diseases (CVD) is lacking. This study examined associations of both long-term summertime temperature and heatwaves as well as short-term extreme temperature with risk of mortality in patients with CVD and its types. We identified new-onset cases of CVD and its specific types including atrial fibrillation, ischemic heart disease (IHD), heart failure and stroke from linked hospital records in the nationwide UK Biobank cohort. Annual summertime heat exposures in terms of mean temperature and annual heatwaves were measured at 1x1 Km 2 spatial resolution. Daily mean temperature and temperature change between neighbouring days (TCN) were measured over lag 0–5 days. Cox proportional hazard model was used to estimate the hazard ratios (HRs) for long-term associations. We used individual-level time stratified case-crossover design to examine short-term associations of mean daily summertime temperature and TCN with mortality. We identified 63,860 patients with new-onset CVD, of which 12,237 (19.2%) died with mean follow-up of 6.1 years. Each 1°C increment in annual mean summertime temperature was associated with 15% higher risk of mortality for CVD patients (HR, 1.15; 95% CI, 1.06-1.24), 10% for atrial fibrillation (1.10; 1.00-1.21), and 19% for IHD (1.19; 1.07-1.33). Risks of mortality remained significantly higher in the group exposed to highest number of annual heatwaves in patients with CVD, and for atrial fibrillation, and heart failure. We identified higher risks of mortality associated with increased summertime temperature in patients of low/moderate (compared with high) education attainment, residing in deprived areas and in neighbourhoods with moderate (compared with high) residential greenspace coverage, suggesting the importance of community planning in climate resilience. Consistently, short-term acute exposure to high temperature was associated with higher risks of mortality for the patient subgroups (OR, 1.70; 95% CI, 1.23-2.34 for CVD; OR, 1.60; 95% CI, 1.05-2.42 for atrial fibrillation and OR, 1.67; 95% CI, 1.04-2.67 for IHD). Similarly, positive TCN was associated with higher odds of mortality among patients with CVD, IHD and heart failure as compared with 0 °C temperature change. Our study found that exposure to extreme summertime temperature is a risk factor for mortality among CVD patients. Planning an appropriate mix of community-based strategies together with personalized adaptations for reducing sensitivity to extreme temperature will constitute vital preventive interventions.

title: Periglacial Landform Distribution and Rock Glacier Dynamics in a Semiarid Andean Headwater Catchment: Estero Derecho Nature Sanctuary, Chile (~30° S)
abstract: ABSTRACT Rock glaciers are key components of high mountain environments, especially in arid and semiarid regions, where glaciers are scarce. These ice‐debris landforms may act as resilient ice reservoirs and have growing hydrological importance under climate warming. Despite their potential significance, rock glaciers in the semiarid Andes remain understudied, and the climatic controls influencing their distribution and activity are poorly understood. This study examines the topoclimatic controls on the distribution and movement of rock glaciers in the Estero Derecho catchment, a semiarid headwater basin in the Chilean Andes. Detailed inventories of periglacial landforms and, specifically, of rock glaciers were developed following the latest standards of the Rock Glacier Inventory and Kinematics (RGIK) committee. By integrating morphometric, kinematic (using spaceborne Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar), and climatic data, the inventory provides a refined classification of rock glacier activity and offers new insights into their environmental controls. We identified and mapped 60 certain rock glaciers. Most were classified as relict landforms (83%), with only three considered active. Current kinematic activity appears to be controlled by morphometric settings and long‐term thermal conditions, which likely preserve internal structure and ground ice of intact landforms. Notably, at around 4500 m a.s.l., there is a shift towards a lower proportion of movement within intact rock glacier areas and a higher mean annual velocity. Overall, short‐term snow cover variations do not influence activity classification but do modulate seasonal and interannual surface displacement. At El Ternero, the largest rock glacier in the area, peak velocities in late summer correlate with snow cover maxima approximately 7 months earlier. A general trend of deceleration from 2017 to 2024 coincides with rising regional temperatures, a higher 0° isotherm, and declining precipitation during the ongoing Megadrought in Central Chile. These findings highlight the complex interplay between long‐term climate constraints and short‐term snow dynamics in controlling the behavior of rock glaciers under changing climatic conditions.

title: GPROF V08: Improving Satellite Precipitation Estimates Across a Heterogeneous Constellation of Passive-Microwave Sensors
abstract: arXiv:2611.19978v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Precipitation estimates from the passive microwave observations (PMW) of the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission serve a wide range of scientific, societal, and economic applications. The Goddard Profiling Algorithm (GPROF) is the operational precipitation retrieval used to produce the level-two precipitation estimates for the GPM mission. This study presents GPROF V08 - the most recent version of GPROF and a major update aimed at improving the accuracy of precipitation estimates from the GPM constellation. GPROF V08 replaces the single-pixel Bayesian retrieval scheme used by earlier GPROF versions with a convolutional neural network (CNN). Implementing the algorithm for the full GPM constellation required addressing several challenges such as the generation of synthetic observations suitable for training CNN retrievals, which has been described in the first part of this two-part study. This second part describes the final, operational implementation of GPROF V08, which adds a finetuning stage to the training to overcome remaining uncertainties in the synthetic training data. We extensively validate the new GPROF V08 algorithm for principal GPM sensors against reference precipitation estimates from combined radar and radiometer retrievals from GPM and TRMM as well as independent ground-based reference measurements. While the magnitude of improvements varies by sensor and surface type, the retrieval accuracy for all assessed sensors is improved. Although challenges such as the persistence of climatological biases (which remain of the same order as for GPROF V07) persist, GPROF V08 constitutes a substantial advancement in spaceborne precipitation monitoring. Since the improvements are robust across all assessed GPM sensors, the update is expected to improve the full historical GPM precipitation record and thus benefit a wide range of downstream datasets and applications.

title: Reconstrução da vegetação dos biomas brasileiros com baixo de CO2 atmosférico e a existência de fogo no Último Máximo Glacial
abstract: O Último Máximo Glacial representa o fim da última glaciação e é marcado pela redução na temperatura média de todo o globo, em comparação as médias atuais. Nesse período, as flutuações climáticas causaram mudanças na vegetação. No entanto, uma análise que leve em consideração a influencia da baixa concentração de dióxido de carbono (CO2) atmosférico e fogo sobre a vegetação são escassos. Frente a isso, o presente estudo pretende reconstruir a vegetação dos biomas brasileiros para cenários distintos, com diferentes nível de CO2 atmosférico e a existência fogo no Último Máximo Glacial (UMG) e no período Pré-Industrial (PI). Para tanto, foi utilizada como metodologia a simulação de reconstruções da cobertura da vegetação, o modelo Land-surface Process and exchanges (LPX), com dados do modelo Miroc de circulação geral da atmosfera. Foram avaliados quatro cenário de reconstrução da vegetação dos biomas brasileiros, para o período pré-industrial e para o UMG, com mudança da variação da concentração atmosférica de CO2 e a existência de incêndios florestais. Os resultados mostraram fragmentação da vegetação, sobretudo para a redução das florestas tropicais e temperadas, com árvores de grandes portes, substituídas por florestas menos adensadas, com dossel aberto ou regiões com vegetação rasteira ou até mesmo desérticas. A hipótese de aparecimento de Refúgios Amazônicos foi verificado. A mudança na concentração do CO2 e a existência de fogo podem acelerar o processo de fragmentação da vegetação dos biomas brasileiros, acelerando o processo de savanização

title: Mobility-driven changes in urban air quality during the COVID-19 lockdown: Evidence from the Baridhara monitoring station, Dhaka, Bangladesh
abstract: by Maheen Zaman, Md. Jobayer Khan, Md. Ahnaf Zaman The COVID-19 lockdown created a natural experiment for examining how large changes in human activity coincided with urban air-quality change. This study evaluated daily Air Quality Index (AQI) and PM2.5 measured at the U.S. Embassy Baridhara monitoring station in northern Dhaka, Bangladesh, using a 2016–2022 air-quality record, Bangladesh-level Google Community Mobility Reports, and NASA POWER meteorological variables. Because the mobility series were available only at national scale, they were treated as contextual proxies for broad activity change rather than as direct measurements of mobility within Dhaka. Four complementary approaches were applied: a SARIMAX interrupted time-series model, partial wavelet coherence, artificial-neural-network weather normalization selected from eight machine-learning models by five-fold time-series cross-validation, and eight mobility-prediction models interpreted with SHAP. The interrupted time series identified a large immediate decline at lockdown onset (AQI −90.3 units; PM2.5 −110.0 µg m − 3; p < 0.001; adjusted R2 = 0.80 and 0.87). After meteorological adjustment, mobility–pollution coherence remained moderate, with the strongest bands at 8–16 days for AQI and 2–4 days for PM2.5. A direct correlation analysis, performed to complement the normalization, showed that the meteorology–pollution relationships of the lockdown months were indistinguishable in sign and magnitude from those of the pre-pandemic and post-lockdown March–June windows. Random Forest best predicted weather-normalized AQI (R2 = 0.60), while XGBoost best predicted weather-normalized PM2.5 (R2 = 0.66); confidence intervals overlapped among leading ensembles. SHAP indicated that residential, grocery and pharmacy, workplace, and transit mobility were the most influential predictors in the fitted models. The findings show a temporary, weather-independent association between broad mobility change and air quality at one monitoring site, but they do not establish a city-wide or causal effect. The results support transport-demand and emissions-management strategies that can deliver local air-quality benefits while complementing climate-mitigation goals.

title: Glacier thickness, thermal regime and subjective uncertainty from ground-penetrating radar of 25 Svalbard glaciers
abstract: Glacier thickness and thermal regime control glacier dynamics and long-term evolution, but observations are sparse at regional scales. These variables can be measured using ground-penetrating radar (GPR), which requires manual or automated interpretation. Interpretation often depends on more than radar signal waveform analysis, yet the resulting subjectivity has not previously been thoroughly quantified. We present 699 km of ground-based GPR data from 25 glaciers in Svalbard, after crowd-sourcing glacier bed and cold-temperate transition surface (CTS) interpretations from 41 contributors. We find that subjective uncertainty is usually smaller than instrument-related uncertainties for the glacier bed, though notable exceptions exist from off-nadir reflections or occlusion by temperate ice. CTS interpretations have higher spreads and show qualitative disagreement in the required amount of scatter to be considered as temperate ice. Our thermal regime consensus estimates reveal a wide diversity in temperate ice extent and distribution between glaciers, as well as insights into the thermal structure of glaciers with surge-related histories. Our thickness consensus agrees with previous measurements, and we show that thickness inversion model performance varies with thermal regime. These data are made available to enable novel applications and automated bed/CTS detection methods that acknowledge interpretation uncertainty.

title: FluidUrban v1.0: enhancing urban ventilation and pollutant dispersion modelling with three-dimensional dynamic adaptive meshes optimisation
abstract: Cities face a major challenge in tracking how wind and air pollution move through complex building clusters. Common numerical models often struggle to balance accuracy with calculating speed. We developed a new simulation system that automatically adjusts its focus to where the air is moving rapidly. By testing this against observations, it significantly improves predictions of wind and pollution. This tool helps urban planners design healthier cities by better identifying how pollutants travel.

title: EGGS-WG: an open source global gridded stochastic  weather generator derived from ERA5-Land
abstract: Stochastic Weather Generators are simple models that can be used to produce realistic, simulated weather. Specifically, they use a combination of statistical techniques and existing measurements to make possible futures. This paper documents the release and provides validation of an open-source modern model, EGGS-WG. It produces daily rainfall values and hourly air temperature and dew point temperature values. The simulation quality is shown to be high when validated against ERA5-Land.

title: Linking ridge shapes to the ice thickness distribution via discrete element simulations
abstract: Sea-ice ridges increase the ice thickness beyond values created by thermodynamic growth as they consist of broken ice pieces piled together. We simulated ridging using a discrete-element-method model, in which the ice is described by individual ice blocks, which can break apart and form ridges. We observe both triangular and trapezoidal ridges. Both ridge shapes influence the amount of thick ice after deformation, which we describe with an analytical function.

title: Development of ACFIRE version 1.0: a mesoscale model with forest canopy and fire behavior submodels
abstract: We introduce a modeling system that couples a surface fire model with a canopy-resolving atmospheric model to simulate two-way fire–atmosphere interactions. Using data from a New Jersey Pine Barrens prescribed burn, we show that the system reproduces observed fire-perturbed atmospheric variables and surface fire spread. Our results demonstrate the potential of dynamic coupling to improve surface fire behavior prediction in complex forests and enable future integration of crown-fire processes.

title: Evaluation of precipitation variability over complex terrain based on observations and high resolution WRF v4.2.2 modelling
abstract: This study compares observed and simulated rainfall in a mountainous area in central Spain from 1991 to 2020. It uses data from high and low elevations, along with long-term simulations and tests at very fine detail. While the finest detail tends to overestimate rainy days, it better captures heavy rainfall events. Overall, the results improve understanding of rainfall patterns and the benefits of higher detail.

title: The stippled grid points are statistically significant: (mis)uses  of false discovery rate correction for geospatial data
abstract: When testing whether signals on maps are statistically meaningful, scientists must account for multiple testing. Otherwise, some results may appear significant purely by chance. We show that the widely used Benjamini–Hochberg correction can be misleading: simply changing the geographic region analyzed can make the same data appear far more statistically significant, even though nothing has changed. We recommend transparent reporting and using region-wide averages instead of pointwise testing.

title: Teleconnection processes linking snow cover variability over western Siberia to enhanced early-winter cold waves in South Korea
abstract: December cold waves in South Korea have become more frequent over the last 46 years, but their drivers remain unclear. We found that reduced October snow cover in western Siberia increases solar absorption and heat release to the atmosphere. This warming is associated with changes in December circulation, favoring northerly winds that bring cold air into East Asia. October snow cover may serve as one of the precursors for early-winter cold waves, potentially helping reduce socioeconomic impacts.

title: Implementation of the reduced complexity model InMAP at  urban scale using a high-resolution WRF-Chem simulation
abstract: In this work, we explored the ability of simpler atmospheric models to analyze the effectiveness of reducing air pollutant emissions to improve air quality. We showed that, despite its simplicity, these models can be used to estimate the areas where impacts will be felt the most, and therefore, can be used by decision makers to maximize the positive impacts of planned air quality improvements.

title: Lake Ice Thickness retrieval using TanDEM-X immediate interferometry
abstract: Given our recent advances in understanding the interaction between lake ice and radar, it has become possible to use radar satellites to measure lake ice thickness. We developed detailed methods for lake ice measurement and compared them with field measurements and thermal-based simulations. Results demonstrated our method can be used to accurately measure ice thickness. The use of recently launched and future satellites is expected to yield more precise measurements using this method.

title: Species-resolved inventory of forest biogenic volatile organic emissions across China with MEGAN v3.2
abstract: To better track natural emissions from forests, we built a detailed model covering 234 tree species across China – far more precise than past methods that lumped all trees into broad categories. The study found that planting different tree species in the same location can produce very different emission patterns, affecting haze and ozone formation in distinct ways. These findings suggest that thoughtful species selection can help balance carbon goals with cleaner air.
